chapter_title: Advanced UV Mapping and Texture Painting
chapter_summary:
Building on our understanding of basic UV unwrapping, let's explore how to refine our UV layouts for maximum efficiency and prepare our models for detailed texture work, including direct painting in Blender. A good unwrap isn't just about avoiding stretching; it's also about optimizing the **UV space** – the 0-1 square in the UV Editor – to ensure consistent texture resolution and make texturing easier.

Once you have your UV islands, the next step is often to **straighten and align** them. Many automatically generated islands might be slightly skewed. In the UV Editor, you can select edges or vertices of an island and use tools like `W > Align Auto` or `Scale > X/Y > 0` (while holding `Shift` to constrain) to make them perfectly horizontal or vertical. This is especially useful for objects with straight lines, like architectural elements or mechanical parts. Straightened UVs are easier to work with in external image editors and result in cleaner textures.

After straightening, you'll want to **pack** your UV islands efficiently. The goal is to fill as much of the 0-1 UV space as possible without overlapping, while maintaining consistent **texel density**. Texel density refers to the number of texture pixels per unit of 3D space. For game assets, it's crucial that all parts of your model have a similar texel density. Otherwise, some areas will look crisp while others appear blurry. Blender has a built-in `Pack Islands` function (`U > Pack Islands` or `UV > Pack Islands` in the UV Editor header) that attempts to arrange your islands. You can also manually move (`G`), rotate (`R`), and scale (`S`) islands to fit them together like puzzle pieces, maximizing the used area. Tools like "Average Island Scale" and "Pack Islands" in the UV menu can help achieve consistent texel density.

Now, let's move to **Texture Painting**. Blender offers powerful tools to paint directly onto your 3D model, which is incredibly useful for adding unique details, wear, dirt, or stylized effects that would be difficult to achieve with tiled textures alone.
1.  **Prepare for Painting:** First, ensure your model has a material with an `Image Texture` node connected to its `Base Color` (or any other channel you want to paint on, like Roughness). This `Image Texture` node needs to have an *actual image* loaded into it, which will serve as your painting canvas. If you don't have one, you can create a new image directly in the `Image Texture` node by clicking "New" and specifying resolution (e.g., 2048x2048 for game assets), color, and alpha. Make sure this image is saved (`Image > Save As` in the UV Editor) to prevent losing your work.
2.  **Enter Texture Paint Mode:** With your object selected, switch from "Object Mode" to "**Texture Paint**" mode in the 3D Viewport header.
3.  **Painting Interface:** You'll immediately see your model in the 3D Viewport ready for painting, and the UV Editor will display your UV map overlaid with your texture. On the left side of the 3D Viewport, you'll find the **Texture Paint Tools** panel, similar to a 2D image editor. Here you can select brushes, adjust brush size (`F`), strength (`Shift + F`), color, and choose between different blend modes.
4.  **Painting Techniques:**
    *   **Direct 3D Painting:** You can paint directly onto the surface of your 3D model in the 3D Viewport. Blender automatically translates your strokes onto the underlying UV map.
    *   **2D UV Painting:** You can also paint directly onto the 2D UV map in the UV Editor. This is useful for precise details or when working on flat, hard-to-reach areas.
    *   **Layers:** While Blender's texture painting isn't layer-based like Photoshop, you can achieve a similar effect by creating multiple `Image Texture` nodes in your Shader Editor, each connected to a `Mix RGB` node, and painting on separate images. This allows for non-destructive workflows.

For game development, texture painting is invaluable for adding unique wear and tear, grime, blood splatters, or custom decals that make an asset feel lived-in and part of the game world. Remember to always save your painted image texture periodically (`Image > Save` or `Alt + S` in the UV Editor) as Blender does not automatically save external image files.

**Common Mistakes and Safety Notes:**
*   **Unsaved Textures:** This is a big one! If you paint for hours and forget to save your image texture (not the Blender file, but the actual image file), all your painting work will be lost when you close Blender. Always save your image texture (`Image > Save As` in the UV Editor) and save it frequently.
*   **Painting on the wrong image:** If you have multiple `Image Texture` nodes, ensure the correct one is selected in the `Image Editor` (or `UV Editor`) and set as the active paint slot in the `Tools` panel (under `Slots`).
*   **Inconsistent Texel Density:** If some UV islands are much smaller than others relative to their 3D size, the texture on those small islands will appear blurry, while others might be crisp. Strive for consistent texel density across your model.
*   **Overlapping UVs and Painting:** If you have overlapping UVs, painting on one area will affect all overlapping areas, which can be problematic if you need unique details. Always ensure unique UVs for unique texture details.
*   **Safety Note on Backup:** Before major texture painting sessions, consider duplicating your model or backing up your Blender file. This provides a safety net if something goes wrong with your painting or UVs.

Mastering advanced UV techniques and texture painting gives you immense creative freedom and control, allowing you to imbue your 3D models with rich, custom details that truly make them stand out in any game.

narration.text: In this lesson we will move beyond basic unwrapping and learn how to make UVs neat, efficient, and ready for detailed texture painting. You will discover why straightening and aligning islands matters, how packing improves texture usage, and what texel density means for consistent visual quality across a model. Then we’ll prepare an image texture, enter Texture Paint mode, and practice painting wear and custom details directly onto a 3D asset. A key practical habit you will form is saving image textures separately from your Blender file so you never lose painted work. By the end you will be able to refine UV islands so they behave predictably in editors, create and save high-resolution paintable images, and apply direct paint strokes that map correctly to your UVs. Think about a wooden crate in a game: consistent texel density keeps all planks sharp, packing fits maximum detail into a single atlas, and painting lets you add believable wear that reads at gameplay distance. Ready to dig in?

narration.text: These learning objectives define the practical skills you will build. First, you will refine UV layouts by straightening, aligning, and packing islands so the UV space is used efficiently and textures behave predictably. For example, aligning island edges removes skew and helps tileable or linear textures sit correctly. Second, you will understand texel density — the ratio of texture pixels to surface area — and how to measure and equalize it so no part of your model looks blurrier than another. Third, you will prepare a model for texture painting by creating and assigning image textures in the material, then ensuring those images are saved externally. Finally, you will use Blender’s Texture Paint mode to apply direct 3D strokes and 2D UV painting, learning brush controls, color, and simple layering via multiple image nodes. Each objective links to a practical step you can perform in Blender and a habit, like saving images, that protects your work.

Practice & Safety Objectives

Work habits that protect your painted images and ensure consistent visual quality.

Save your image

After creating or painting an image, use Image > Save As and give it a meaningful filename tied to your project folder.

screens.title: UV Layouts and Optimization
screens.subtitle: Why good UV packing and layout matter for texture quality

narration.text: A clean UV layout is the foundation of consistent, efficient texturing. UV islands map 3D surface regions into the 0-1 UV square, and how you place and scale those islands determines how many texture pixels cover each surface. The primary goal is twofold: avoid stretching and maximize use of UV space without overlaps. Consider a set of modular planks: if one plank's island is much smaller than another, it will receive fewer pixels and appear blurrier in-game. Packing islands tightly reduces wasted empty space and lets you allocate more pixels to important features. But packing is not purely automatic — sometimes manual rotation and scaling are necessary to fit awkward shapes like curved joints. A common misconception is that a denser pack automatically equals better quality; instead, consistent texel density matters more than packing density alone. In practice, you will straighten islands when applicable, run Average Island Scale to normalize sizes, then pack so the most visible parts get prioritized. What surface on your model needs the highest resolution, and how will you allocate UV space accordingly? UV Layouts and Optimization means prioritize consistent texel density and strategic packing so visible parts receive sufficient texture resolution.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › UV Layouts
Definition

What a UV layout does

A UV layout unfolds the 3D surface into flat islands inside the 0-1 square so a 2D image can paint color and detail onto the model.

Why it matters
Good layouts avoid stretching, allow predictable painting, and enable efficient use of texture pixels.
Concrete example
If a character's face island is too small, facial details will blur. Increase its island scale or allocate more UV space.
Key takeaway
Match UV scale to importance; pack carefully to maximize useful pixels without overlaps.
Visual guide
Packing trade-off
  • Tighter packing uses more pixels but must keep islands non-overlapping.
  • Some larger islands should be reserved for high-detail surfaces.
  • Manual rotation and scaling help fit difficult shapes.
Common misconception
Packing alone does not guarantee visual consistency. Always normalize texel density first so islands represent surface area fairly.

screens.title: Straightening and Aligning UV Islands
screens.subtitle: Tools and hands-on steps to make islands clean and predictable

narration.text: Straightening and aligning UV islands reduces skew and makes textures easier to paint and tile. Begin by selecting an island in the UV Editor and inspect its edges; if a set of edges should be straight, select the vertices and use Align Auto or use Scale constrained to an axis to flatten them. For example, select a table leg’s seam vertices, press Scale then X or Y then 0 while holding Shift to keep control; this makes edges perfectly vertical or horizontal. Another practical method is to select an edge and use the Align tool from the UV menu to match a target. After straightening, rotate islands to align their primary direction to horizontal or vertical so brush strokes and baked patterns read consistently. A typical workflow: identify linear geometry, straighten with Align or Scale axis=0, rotate the island for easier packing, then nudge vertices as needed. A common mistake is over-straightening curved geometry; do not force smooth organic shapes into perfect lines, as that introduces distortion. Always preview the result by checking the 3D Viewport for stretching. Which edges on your model should remain straight, and which should preserve curvature?

keyIdea.title: Straighten skill
keyIdea.text: Use Align Auto and axis-constrained scaling to make straight edges and improve painting predictability while preserving intended curvature.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Straighten & Align
Step-by-step

Straighten an island

  1. Select the island or specific vertices you want to align in the UV Editor.
  2. Use W > Align Auto or press S then X (or Y) then 0 while holding Shift to snap to an axis.
  3. Rotate (R) so the island's main direction is horizontal or vertical for predictable painting.
  4. Check the 3D Viewport for stretching and adjust vertices if necessary.
Concrete example
Straighten a crate plank edge so wood grain brushes run parallel and details tile cleanly.
Pro tip
Only straighten sections that are physically straight. Keep organic curves unaltered to avoid stretching artifacts.
Visual checklist
  • Select vertices, align, scale axis = 0, rotate island.
  • Preview in 3D, look for seams and stretching, iteratively tweak.
  • Don't over-constrain curved geometry; preserve form where needed.
Key Takeaway
Use axis-constrained scaling and align tools to make predictable islands that simplify painting and text placement.

screens.title: Packing UV Islands Efficiently
screens.subtitle: Strategies and tools to maximize 0-1 UV usage without overlaps

narration.text: Packing UV islands places your unfolded pieces inside the 0-1 square to use as much texture area as possible. Blender's Pack Islands is a helpful starting point, but it is a heuristic — after running it you often need manual tweaks. Begin by selecting all islands and using UV → Average Island Scale to normalize relative sizes so texels map consistently. Then run Pack Islands (U → Pack Islands) to let Blender arrange them. Inspect the results: rotate and nudge islands manually to fill awkward gaps and prioritize important parts by scaling them slightly larger before re-packing. For a modular set intended to share a texture atlas, align similar parts and pack them together to conserve space and simplify material usage. One practical approach is to run several pack attempts with different island priorities, saving a backup between runs. A misconception to avoid is uniformly scaling every island to fill space; that breaks texel density. Instead, normalize first, then selectively prioritize visible assets. How would you prioritize islands for a character versus a prop? Packing UV Islands Efficiently means average island scale, then pack, then manual prioritize and scale important islands for best texture allocation.. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Pack Islands
Workflow

Pack islands without breaking texel density

  1. Use Average Island Scale to normalize island sizes relative to surface area.
  2. Run UV → Pack Islands to get an automatic arrangement.
  3. Manually rotate and move islands to fill gaps and prioritize visible areas.
  4. Scale high-importance islands slightly before re-packing if needed, but keep overall density consistent.
Example
For a set of props, pack related planks together in one region of the atlas so they share similar shading and can be tiled consistently.
Common mistake
Scaling islands indiscriminately after packing creates inconsistent texel density and uneven visual sharpness.
Visual tips
  • Prioritize faces seen up close; give them more UV area.
  • Group similar materials or tiled areas to reduce wasted space.
  • Save iterations so you can compare pack outcomes and revert if necessary.
Key Takeaway
Combine average scaling with manual packing to balance density and visual importance across your model.

screens.title: Texel Density Explained
screens.subtitle: What texel density is, why it matters, and how to equalize it

narration.text: Texel density is the ratio of texture pixels to units of 3D surface area. Practically, it tells you how many texture pixels correspond to a meter, centimeter, or model unit on your asset. Consistent texel density across all parts of an asset ensures a uniform perceived sharpness. For example, if a character's torso has twice the texel density of the arms, the torso will look much sharper in the game while the arms look blurry. To equalize texel density, use Average Island Scale in Blender after unwrapping. Another approach is to measure pixels per unit manually and scale islands so their pixel-per-unit matches a target value, such as 10 px/cm for a particular project. A common misconception is that higher texel density everywhere is always better. Instead, allocate higher density only to visible or focal areas and save pixels where the player won't notice. The key practice is to choose a target density for the project and normalize islands to match that target before packing into an atlas. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Texel Density
Definition

What texel density means

Texel density is the count of texture pixels mapped per unit of surface area. It defines visual resolution across the model.

Concrete example
If a plank receives 1024 pixels across 1 meter and another plank receives 512, the first will appear twice as sharp.
When to vary density
Give more density to focal areas like faces or player-visible surfaces and reduce density on distant or hidden parts.
Practical steps
  1. Decide on a project target (e.g., px per meter or px per cm).
  2. Use Average Island Scale to equalize island sizes by surface area.
  3. Manually scale visible islands up and less visible ones down before packing.
Key Takeaway
Consistent texel density creates uniform sharpness; prioritize visible surfaces when allocating pixels.

screens.title: Preparing an Image Texture for Painting
screens.subtitle: Create an image texture, connect it to a material, and save it safely

narration.text: Before you can paint, Blender needs an actual image file connected to the material. Start in the Shader Editor: select your material and add an Image Texture node. If no image exists, click New to create one. Choose a sensible resolution such as 2048x2048 for game assets, pick a neutral base color if you like, and name the file clearly — for example, crate_basecolor_paint. After creating or loading the image, connect it to the Base Color input so your material shows the texture. This image lives in Blender’s memory until you explicitly save it. Use Image → Save As in the UV Editor to write the painted image to disk. A common mistake is relying on the Blender file save alone; the external image file must be saved separately or your paint will be lost on close. As a practical habit, save your image immediately after creation and again periodically while you paint. Which name and resolution will you choose for your next painted texture? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Image Texture Prep
Steps

Create and save a paintable image

  1. Open Shader Editor, add an Image Texture node and click New if no image exists.
  2. Set resolution (e.g., 2048x2048), name it clearly, and choose a base color if desired.
  3. Connect the Image Texture node to the Base Color of your material.
  4. Open the UV Editor and choose Image → Save As to write the file to disk immediately.
Concrete example
Create crate_basecolor_paint at 2048x2048 and save it to your project folder before the first stroke.
Warning
Not saving the image means your painting exists only in memory and will be lost when Blender closes.
Checklist
  • Name the image clearly and include resolution in the filename if helpful.
  • Save to disk immediately and periodically while painting.
  • Confirm the image is selected as the active paint slot in the Tools panel.
Key Takeaway
Never rely on the .blend save for painted images; always write your image files to disk explicitly.

screens.title: Entering Texture Paint Mode & Interface
screens.subtitle: How to access painting tools and control brushes in Blender

narration.text: Texture Paint mode turns the 3D Viewport into a canvas mapped to your UVs. To enter it, select your object and switch the mode dropdown to Texture Paint. The Tools panel exposes brushes similar to a 2D editor: Draw, Blur, Smear, and so on. Use F to adjust brush radius and Shift + F to change strength. Color pick allows quick sampling from the viewport or the UV Editor. When you paint in 3D Viewport, Blender projects strokes onto the underlying UV map so your 3D strokes correspond to 2D pixels. You can also paint directly in the UV Editor for exact control on flat regions. A helpful workflow is to use 3D painting for intuitive strokes and switch to 2D UV painting for precise decals or logos. Common mistakes include forgetting to set the active image slot and painting onto the wrong image, or using very large brush strength for subtle details. Before you begin a long paint session, confirm brush hotkeys and save your image. How will you combine 3D freedom with 2D precision on your asset? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Texture Paint Mode
Quick start

Access brushes and paint controls

  • Switch object mode to Texture Paint with the object selected.
  • Open the Tools panel to pick Draw, Blur, Smear, etc.
  • Use F to change brush radius and Shift + F to change strength in real time.
  • Ensure the active image slot is the one you want to modify.
3D vs 2D
Paint in 3D for organic strokes, switch to UV Editor to place precise decals or correct seams.
Tip
Use mirrored painting cautiously; overlapping UVs will mirror strokes to all overlapped regions.
Brush controls
- F : change radius
- Shift + F : change strength
- Color picker: sample from viewport or UV Editor
Key Takeaway
Master F and Shift + F and confirm the active image slot to paint confidently and avoid accidental strokes.

screens.title: 3D Painting vs 2D UV Painting
screens.subtitle: When to paint on the model and when to paint on the UV map

narration.text: There are two complementary painting approaches in Blender. Direct 3D painting lets you stroke naturally across the surface and see results in context; Blender projects your strokes onto the UVs. This is fastest for organic wear, dirt, and general shading because you can rotate the model and paint where it reads visually. 2D UV painting in the UV Editor gives pixel-accurate control over seams, logos, and crisp decals because you work directly on the flattened island. Use 3D painting when you want fast, intuitive results that follow surface curvature; use 2D painting for precise placement and seam fixes. A common misconception is that one method is strictly better. Instead, combine them: block in shapes with 3D strokes and finish or correct edges and small details in the UV Editor. When you need a sharp logo on a crate face, paint it in the UV Editor. When you want soft grime along edges, paint in 3D. keyIdea.text: Use 3D painting for organic strokes and speed; use 2D UV painting for precise decals, seams, and pixel-perfect details.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › 3D vs 2D
3D Painting

Intuitive surface strokes

  • Paint directly on the model; brushes follow curvature.
  • Best for broad wear, dirt, and soft transitions.
  • Quick feedback in the scene context.
Example: Use 3D to add grime along the bottom edges of a crate so it reads naturally from all angles.
2D UV Painting

Pixel-accurate control

  • Paint on the flattened UV map for crisp edges.
  • Best for decals, logos, and seam cleanup.
  • Useful when exact pixel placement matters.
Example: Place a painted brand logo on a single crate face by drawing it directly on the UV island for that face.
Key Takeaway
Combine both methods: block broad strokes in 3D, refine and place precise details in the UV Editor for the best results.

screens.title: Layering Strategies and Non-destructive Painting
screens.subtitle: Using multiple image nodes and Mix RGB to simulate layers

narration.text: Blender’s texture painting is not layer-based like a 2D editor, but you can simulate non-destructive layers by using multiple Image Texture nodes combined with Mix nodes. The pattern is simple: create separate images for base color, dirt, decals, and small detail layers. In the Shader Editor, connect each Image Texture node through a Mix RGB node in the desired blend order so each layer contributes to the final Base Color. When you need to edit a specific element, paint directly into its corresponding image file. This approach keeps the base and detail separate and makes it easy to iterate or replace a worn layer without reworking the whole texture. A common pitfall is forgetting to set the correct image node active in the paint slot; you may paint on the wrong image and overwrite a different layer. Another tip is to keep a flattened backup image that combines all layers so you have a single composite for export while preserving layer images for future edits. Which parts of your workflow would benefit from a separate dirt layer versus painting directly on the base?

keyIdea.title: Layering workflow
keyIdea.text: Use multiple image nodes and Mix RGB nodes to create editable layers, painting each image separately and keeping a flattened backup for export.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Layering
Approach

Simulate layers with images and Mix nodes

  1. Create separate images for base, dirt, decals, etc.
  2. In the Shader Editor, chain Image Texture nodes through Mix RGB nodes to blend them.
  3. Paint on each image independently as needed and keep a flattened composite backup for export.
Example
Use a separate 'dirt' image to add grime. If you need to adjust intensity, tweak the Mix factor instead of repainting.
Pitfall
Painting without selecting the right image node overwrites another layer. Confirm the active slot before painting.
Checklist
  • Name each image by purpose: base, dirt, decals.
  • Keep a final flattened copy for engine export.
  • Use Mix node factors to tune layer influence non-destructively.
Key Takeaway
Layer by image and blend with Mix nodes so edits stay localized and reversible.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.subtitle: Protect your work and avoid painting pitfalls

narration.text: There are a few recurring mistakes that cost time and unrecoverable work. The most significant is not saving the painted image file. The. blend may be saved while the image remains only in memory, and closing Blender loses that image. Always use Image → Save or Save As in the UV Editor. Another issue is painting on the wrong image slot when multiple Image Texture nodes exist; verify the active slot in the Tools panel. Overlapping UVs cause mirrored painting — useful for symmetry but harmful when you need unique detail; ensure unique UVs for unique paint. Inconsistent texel density creates areas that look blurry or overly sharp; normalize sizes with Average Island Scale before packing. Finally, avoid over-compressing textures for a final export step; test your game engine import to ensure visual fidelity. A simple habit prevents many problems: before every paint session, confirm the active image, save it, and take a quick backup. After that, you can paint confidently. In practical terms, protect your work and avoid painting pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Common Mistakes
Major mistakes
  • Unsaved textures: Always use Image → Save As and save frequently.
  • Wrong paint slot: Confirm active image node in the Tools panel before strokes.
  • Overlapping UVs: Overlaps mirror paint and prevent unique details.
  • Inconsistent texel density: Use Average Island Scale to normalize before packing.
Practical safety: before long sessions, save your image, save a backup .blend copy, and verify slots and UV uniqueness.
Quick recovery
- Save images frequently (Alt + S in UV Editor).
- Keep incremental backups of your project folder.
- Export flattened copies for engine import while keeping editable layers.
Final warning
Losing painted images is common but avoidable; save images and back up before major changes.

screens.title: Activity: Paint Wear and Tear on a Wooden Crate
screens.subtitle: A guided step-by-step exercise to practice the full workflow

narration.text: This hands-on exercise walks you through creating a paintable image, entering Texture Paint, and adding wear to a crate. Start with your unwrapped crate from the previous exercise. In the Shader Editor, confirm your Base Color has an Image Texture; if not, create a new image named crate_basecolor_paint at 2048x2048 and save it to your project folder. Switch to Texture Paint mode. Choose the Draw brush, pick a darker brown for grime, and use F and Shift + F to adjust size and strength. Paint along edges and corners to simulate wear; these strokes will appear on the UV map simultaneously. For subtle highlights, use a light brown at low strength. If you need a precise logo on a board face, switch to the UV Editor and paint the logo directly on that island. Periodically use Image → Save in the UV Editor to write your changes to disk. After painting, save a flattened copy for export but keep individual layer images if you used separate image nodes. Reflect: which brush settings gave the most believable edge wear? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Crate Painting Activity
Steps
  1. Ensure an Image Texture is connected to Base Color; create crate_basecolor_paint at 2048x2048 and save.
  2. Switch to Texture Paint mode and select the Draw brush.
  3. Use a darker color for grime along edges; adjust F and Shift + F for size and strength.
  4. Use lighter, low-strength strokes for subtle highlights and scratches.
  5. Switch to the UV Editor for precise logo placement or seam fixes.
  6. Save the image frequently and export a flattened copy for the engine while keeping editable images for future edits.
Example settings
- Grime: Radius ~ 80 px, Strength 0.4
- Scratches: Radius ~ 12 px, Strength 0.2, light color
- Save image: Image → Save or Alt + S in UV Editor
Key Takeaway
Practice a cycle: create, save, paint, save, and export. This keeps work safe and iterative.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Here are the core concepts to retain. Texel density determines visual sharpness; pick a project target and normalize islands to match it. Pack Islands arranges your islands inside the 0-1 space for efficient texture use but should follow texel normalization and manual prioritization. Straightening UVs makes linear geometry and tiling textures behave predictably and reduces awkward seams. These are practical, repeatable ideas: normalize, straighten, pack, then paint and save. Keep these steps in your pipeline and the outcomes will be textures that look consistent and robust in a game environment. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Texel Density
Pixels per unit of surface area. Match across islands for uniform sharpness.
Pack Islands
Arrange islands inside 0-1 to maximize useful texture area without overlaps.
Straighten UVs
Align edges and vertices for cleaner tiling and easier painting.
Takeaway

A disciplined sequence — normalize density, straighten where appropriate, pack deliberately, create and save images, then paint — produces consistent, high-quality textures.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Tools & Workflows
screens.subtitle: Short reminders of tools and common workflow checks

narration.text: Remember the practical tools and checks: Average Island Scale equalizes island sizes for consistent texel density. Pack Islands arranges pieces inside the 0-1 square but requires manual refinement. Texture Paint mode enables direct painting and the UV Editor allows precise edits and logo placement. Finally, always save the image texture file externally; Blender does not guarantee image saves with the. blend alone. Keep these tool reminders in mind during your painting sessions to avoid common pitfalls and to produce reliable game-ready textures. Average Island Scale
